1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle. But after his departure they were tempted by false apostles, to be turned to the law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to the faith of truth, writing to them from Ephesus. Paul, an apostle. By the name of his office he strikes terror. Not of men. Understand: of apostles, as certain pseudo-apostles chosen and sent by the Jews. Neither by man. But by Jesus now risen. Who taught not as man teaches men little by little, but the whole at once by the Spirit: so that he is greater in that in which he seemed less. For the other apostles seemed greater because they were first. This one the least, because last. But from this he appears more worthy: because the first were appointed through Christ still partly man, that is mortal. But Paul, the last, through Christ now wholly God, that is in every part immortal.
1.2: 1.2 Who are with me. The Christian brethren grieve over your seduction, witnesses of my truth, whom you ought to believe, and not a few, but all.
1.3: 1.3 And the Lord Jesus Christ. Whom you injuriously equate with the law, while you assert that he is not sufficient for salvation without the law: just as the law without him: but from him, without the law, is grace and peace.
1.4: 1.4 Who gave. That is, offered of his own will: because there is no other who could open the book but the lion of the tribe of Judah. Himself. Because there was no other victim worthy for blotting out our sins, which is the beginning of salvation. What place then has the law? As if to say: None at all. From the world. That is from conformity to the world, which allures us. From this present wicked world. The more it takes hold, since eternal things are not seen. Wicked world. He says this not because this world created by God is evil, but because evils are done in it. And in this sense it is said: The days are evil. The world is seated in the wicked one. Dangerous times. Forest passes full of robbers, and the sword with which blood is shed, and the cup in which poison is mixed, are called evil: because not only times, but also places and instruments of evils have drawn infamy from the things done in them.
1.5: 1.5 To whom be glory. As if to say: The good now present bear witness to this, and those to come will bear witness. In this salvation he gave a foretaste both of his own commendation, and of what the grace of God can do, and that the law confers nothing.
1.6: 1.6 I wonder. The Apostle consequently treats of the destruction of the law. And he rebukes them for fickleness, that they passed indiscriminately from the Gospel to the law. And because Galatia means translation, he fittingly takes from the very name an occasion of rebuke. And since these good things aforesaid are from Christ, I wonder that, well instructed before, you are so, so vehemently and in so short a time, transferred, etc.
1.8: 1.8 But though we, etc. A good angel may be understood, not that this happens, but he is so certain of the truth of his Gospel that if even an angel should announce otherwise, he would not believe but would anathematize. Besides that. AUGUSTINE. Attend. He does not say: More than you have received. For if he said that, he would prejudge himself, who desired to come to some to whom he himself wrote: as to the Thessalonians, that he might supply what was lacking to their faith. But he who supplies adds what was lacking; he does not take away what was in it. But he who goes beyond the rule of faith does not advance on the way, but departs from the way. Let him be anathema. Why this? Because he who preaches otherwise wishes to flow from his own, not from the common source. And since a man hindered by a carnal mist and led back from the common fountain to his own falsity can do this, can an angel not also? Truly, if an angel flowing from his own had not been heard in paradise, we should not have been hurled into death. The commandment of God was set in the midst for all. It was in a way public water, and flowed without fraud, without stain, without mud. But the angel came, fallen from heaven, made a serpent, because he already desired to spread his poison by guile, and sent forth the poison. He spoke from his own, from himself: Taste, and you shall be as gods, Genesis 3. And they, seeking what they were not, lost what they had received. Anathema. This word is used for cursed, and is commonly called devotion. For hardly anyone says he devotes himself, unless cursing himself. Whence that: And he anathematized him and his cities, and the name of that place was called Anathema, Numbers 21. Hence it came about that anathema seems something detestable and abominable, so that the victor should carry off nothing of it for his own uses, but devoted the whole to be paid in punishment: this was to anathematize, which is commonly called to devote. The origin of this word, however, is in the Greek language, from the things that, vowed and paid, that is promised and rendered, were set up on high in the temples: and it is said: that is, to set up on high.
1.9: 1.9 As we have said before. He infers from the greater. Since we or an angel would be excommunicated, much more are the pseudo-apostles to be excommunicated.
1.10: 1.10 Now. He says now because formerly, when he said that man is justified by the law, he preached the glory of man as useless, the grace of God as useful. He hints here that those seducers also do this, that they may be praised by the Jews, whom Paul does not fear to offend for the glory of Christ, at whose coming the law ceases. If I yet. Hence some think conscience suffices, so that they care little what another thinks of them; but conscience before God is necessary, conduct before one's neighbor also; which, if carried on more carelessly, harms by example. Hence elsewhere: Please all men in all things, as I also please all men in all things, 2 Corinthians 10. Likewise: Be without offense to the Jews and to the Greeks and to the Church of God, 2 Corinthians 8. Likewise: Providing good things, not only before God, but also before men, Matthew 5. Likewise: Let your works shine before men, etc. Therefore, against rash judges, detractors, whisperers, murmurers, who seek to suspect what they do not see, who seek even to boast of what they do not suspect, conscience suffices. Nor in others, whom we wish to please, let us seek our own glory, but their salvation, that they may praise not us, but God, who made such men; hence: Do not your justice before men, where he rebukes those who so fan their works that they make the praise of men the end of their works, and reckon the same praise as the reward of their works.
